patient.name: Dominic Ruiz
patient.chiefComplaint: Unresponsive, not breathing after high-speed single-vehicle MVC

history.hpi: 28-year-old male involved in a high-speed single-vehicle collision into a fixed tree. A bystander witnessed brief spontaneous movement and vocalization immediately after impact, followed by rapid loss of responsiveness and cessation of breathing approximately 4 minutes prior to EMS arrival — meeting criteria for a witnessed traumatic cardiac arrest with recent signs of life.
pastMedical: Unknown — unresponsive patient, no bystander history available
history.events: High-speed single-vehicle MVC into a fixed tree; bystander witnessed brief movement/vocalization followed by cardiac arrest approximately 4 minutes prior to EMS arrival

scene.dispatch: 28-year-old male, motor vehicle collision, unknown status, single vehicle off roadway
scene.location: Rural two-lane highway, single vehicle struck a tree at high speed; patient found partially ejected onto the shoulder
scene.safety: Vehicle stable off roadway, no active fire, fuel leak controlled by fire crew, scene lighting limited
scene.bystanders: A passing motorist stopped after witnessing the crash and reports the patient was moving and moaning immediately after impact but became still and stopped breathing before EMS arrival, approximately 4 minutes ago
visualCues: Severe front-end vehicle deformation with steering wheel deformity
Patient supine on shoulder, pale, no visible chest rise
Bruising across both sides of the anterior chest wall
Pelvis appears grossly unstable on visual inspection

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 28-year-old male supine on the roadway shoulder following a high-speed MVC. He is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. A bystander confirms brief movement and vocalization immediately post-crash before he went still — a witnessed arrest with recent signs of life, meeting criteria for traumatic cardiac arrest management.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but no spontaneous respiratory effort
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic, no chest rise, breath sounds not yet assessed
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable central or peripheral pulses
otherFindings: Bilateral anterior chest wall bruising consistent with steering wheel impact
Bystander confirms brief movement/vocalization immediately post-crash

expectedActions.shortAction: Assess for signs of life: pulses, respiratory effort, other signs
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assess for signs of life, including pulses, respiratory effort, and evaluation of other signs of life
expectedActions.rationale: Confirms arrest status and distinguishes traumatic arrest from a patient with pulses who instead needs General Trauma Management.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Resuscitation in Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

expectedActions.shortAction: Control any external hemorrhage with tourniquet or hemostatic wound packing
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Place tourniquets for wounds amenable to tourniquet placement
expectedActions.rationale: Massive hemorrhage is a leading reversible cause of traumatic arrest and must be addressed first.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Resuscitation in Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply pelvic binder for the grossly unstable pelvis
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Place a pelvic binder on all patients with blunt or blast trauma suffering traumatic arrest
expectedActions.rationale: An unstable pelvis is a major internal hemorrhage source that a binder can control noninvasively.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Resuscitation in Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

expectedActions.shortAction: Perform bilateral rapid needle chest decompression
expectedActions.rationale: Absent breath sounds and blunt chest trauma raise concern for bilateral tension pneumothorax, a rapidly reversible cause of PEA arrest.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Resuscitation in Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

expectedActions.rationale: Vascular access is required for volume resuscitation targeting hypovolemia as a reversible cause.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Resuscitation in Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate 500 mL crystalloid bolus, reassess and repeat as needed
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If SBP less than 90 mmHg or HR greater than 120 BPM, initiate resuscitation: ... consider 500 mL bolus of IV fluid, repeat as needed for persistent signs and symptoms of shock
expectedActions.rationale: Volume resuscitation addresses hypovolemia while blood products are unavailable in the field.

transitions.if: Primary survey and bilateral decompression performed
transitions.condition: Crew performs a rapid primary survey targeting reversible causes: hemorrhage control, airway management, bilateral needle chest decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax, and IV/IO access with volume resuscitation.
Crew focuses on CPR and standard resuscitation without performing bilateral needle chest decompression despite absent breath sounds and chest trauma, missing the reversible cause of the arrest.

phases.name: Primary survey and bilateral decompression performed
phases.description: Crew works through the traumatic arrest reversible-causes sequence: hemorrhage control, pelvic binder placement, bilateral rapid needle chest decompression, and IV/IO access with volume resuscitation. Rush of air is noted bilaterally on decompression.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing a witnessed traumatic arrest with recent signs of life, the crew proceeds directly to reversible-cause management rather than standard ACLS: hemorrhage control, pelvic binder, bilateral needle decompression, and IV/IO access with fluids.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Managed with BVM, adjunct in place
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Bilateral breath sounds now audible after decompression, chest rise with BVM ventilation
otherFindings: Bilateral needle decompression performed, rush of air noted on both sides
Pelvic binder applied for unstable pelvis
IO access established, crystalloid bolus running

expectedActions.shortAction: Minimize scene time, transport rapidly to the highest-level trauma center
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with major hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, penetrating torso trauma, or signs of traumatic brain injury often require rapid surgical intervention. Minimize scene time (goal is under 10 minutes) and initiate rapid transport to the highest level of care within the trauma system
expectedActions.rationale: Post-ROSC traumatic arrest patients need definitive surgical hemorrhage control that only a trauma center can provide.

transitions.condition: After hemorrhage control, pelvic binder, bilateral decompression, and IV/IO fluid resuscitation, the rhythm organizes and a palpable pulse returns.

phases.name: Reversible causes addressed, pulses return
phases.description: Following bilateral decompression and volume resuscitation, the patient regains a palpable pulse with an organized tachycardic rhythm. He remains unresponsive and ventilator-dependent but is now perfusing. Crew prepares for rapid transport.
phases.triggerCondition: After bilateral needle decompression relieves tension physiology and volume resuscitation restores circulating volume, spontaneous circulation returns with a palpable radial pulse and measurable blood pressure.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Managed with BVM, adjunct in place
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Assisted ventilation, bilateral breath sounds equal
otherFindings: Pelvic binder and decompression sites stable
Prepared for rapid transport to trauma center

phases.name: Bilateral decompression delayed or skipped
phases.description: The crew performs CPR and standard resuscitation measures but does not perform bilateral needle chest decompression despite absent breath sounds and significant chest trauma. Tension physiology continues to worsen and the rhythm deteriorates.
phases.triggerCondition: Crew delays or omits bilateral needle chest decompression despite absent breath sounds and blunt chest trauma; the unrelieved tension physiology prevents any return of circulation, and the rhythm deteriorates from PEA to asystole.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Managed with BVM, adjunct in place
clinicalPresentation.breathing: No chest rise on the affected side despite BVM ventilation
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable pulses despite ongoing CPR

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize unrelieved tension physiology; perform bilateral needle decompression immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If absent or diminished breath sounds in a hypotensive trauma patient, especially those with chest trauma and/or tracheal deviation, consider tension pneumothorax and perform needle decompression of side without breath sounds or side opposite tracheal deviation; may need second or third needle decompression on same side if there is a rush of air but patient again has symptoms
expectedActions.rationale: Persistent absent breath sounds with worsening arrest physiology signals an unaddressed reversible cause that must be corrected immediately.
